articles.title: Farmers in India call for another national mobilization
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Farmers unions in India, under the banner of the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM), have called for a nationwide mobilization to protest the attempt to open the country’s agricultural market for foreign competition without addressing the problems they’ve been facing for years. The protests will mark the sixth anniversary of the 2020-21 protests, in which thousands of farmers had camped on the borders of the capital, New Delhi, for months, forcing the government to withdraw farm laws and promise to address other agricultural issues. Read more: Indian farmers celebrate victory march back home as their historic struggle ends after a year The SKM was born as a united front of farmers unions, representing millions, during the struggle against the three farm laws. In a press release issued on Monday, November 9, SKM claimed that the Modi government has not fulfilled a single promise it made while signing the agreement with the farmers six years ago, which led to the suspension of the movement. “In 2020, farmers numbering in the hundreds of thousands fought the pro-corporate three farm laws. In the signed agreement of December 9, 2021, farmers were given hope that the government will solve” their problems. However, they have been betrayed, SKM said in the press release. Their main demands include enacting a law for the minimum support price (MSP) for all farm products on the basis of the total cost of production + 50% profit formula, scrap all the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) signed with the European Union, the UK, and New Zealand along with the proposed FTA with the US, and the restoration of the rural employment guarantee law withdrawn recently. The Modi government’s FTAs with Europe and the US will open India’s agricultural markets to highly subsidized agricultural goods which will ultimately harm the livelihoods of millions in India dependent on farming. These farmers are already struggling to continue farming due to rising input prices and the lack of enough return, SKM and other farmers’ unions had said earlier. The November 26 agitation will include the demands of the workers’ unions in the country to scrap four new labor codes introduced earlier this year by the Modi government. The laws are widely seen as an attack on the workers’ basic rights, such as eight hours of work and collective bargaining. Defending democracy The farmers are also supporting the ongoing national agitation against the alleged electoral malpractices in the country. The SKM has also demanded the removal of the country’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of manipulating elections to help the ruling far-right BJP win. SKM’s press release called for the cancellation of the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and re-inclusion of all the 130 million plus voters removed from the country’s electoral lists through it so far. According to the opposition, most of the voters removed from the electoral lists through the SIR have conventionally voted against the ruling ultra-right-wing and Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). They allege that the mass removal of voters was part of the deliberate attempt of the CEC to tilt elections in favor of the BJP. Youth and students groups, along with the opposition parties, have faced massive state crackdown for launching a nationwide movement in October demanding the scrapping of the SIR and sacking Gyanesh Kumar. Farmer’s unions will organize protests at various locations across the country before coming to the capital, Delhi, on November 26 and march to the Parliament while also challenging the Modi government’s attempts to curb popular protests. The November 26 march is set to culminate at the Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which has been recently denotified by the government as a protest site making it a criminal offense to organize a protest there.

articles.title: France’s protest movement is fighting more than Macron
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Macron offered “crumbs.” France answered with a general strike against austerity that brought the country to a standstill and more than 1.6 million people to the streets. Iman D., a student organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, was on the ground at the Paris protests. She tells Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek the multinational, multigenerational movement behind the shutdown names capitalism as the problem, not just Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Iman explains why Nov. 5 general strikers carried Palestinian flags and wore keffiyehs, and unpacks how Black and Arab youth from the suburbs – the children and grandchildren of the people France colonized – helped spark the uprising. She recounts a visit to a high school in Saint-Denis, where students described unchecked Islamophobia, from the school hijab ban to police abductions from classrooms, and a system that pours money into war while their schools crumble. It’s “continued colonialism,” they say, carried out by forces descended from those that brutalized their grandparents in Algeria. A Minnesota organizer herself, Iman draws the line from Paris to the Minneapolis general strikes against ICE’s Operation Metro Surge. And after the midterms’ blue tsunami that won Democrats control of Congress, she stresses now’s not the time to settle for crumbs: “It’s mass movements that really create change.” #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1:] The people of France truly understand that their fight against racism, anti-Blackness, anti-Muslim fascism, and state violence is tied to Palestine. They’re aware that the same system funding the war in the streets of France against Black and Arab youth is the same system funding genocide and imperialism abroad. They see and understand their struggle as one. Nationwide protests against austerity have continued in France following the massive general strike on November 5th when 1.6 million people took to the streets. Protests are taking place across the country even today, November 10th, and they’re also planned for November 14th, 17th, and 19th. People are not stopping this struggle against austerity and to demand an end to the cuts-based policies put forward by Emmanuel Macron and the government of Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne. Students, trade unionists, and pensioners are all demanding that this government takes seriously the long set of demands they have presented to Macron and Borne. As of now, all of these groups, especially the student movement, have dismissed the offers of dialogue and proposals from this government as crumbs. That’s why they’re staying on the streets. To discuss this massive uprising that has been quite inspirational for people across the world, we are very excited to be joined by Iman D. She is a student organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, and she was on the streets last week in Paris speaking to people about why they’re out there. So Iman, thank you so much for joining us. [Iman D:] Yes, thank you so much, Rania and Zoe. Super excited to join you all today. [Speaker 1:] Iman, you were in Paris last week, witnessing history. Let’s be honest. You saw the general strike which took place on November 5th. Again, there were 1.6 million people according to trade unions that participated in mobilizations on this day. So talk to us first about your impressions of this strike. What was the mood on the streets? And what was it like speaking to people? [Iman D:] Thank you again. On November 5th, France had a general strike, and I had the opportunity to be on the ground and witness it. I don’t even know where to begin. I don’t think I or any American has ever witnessed something at that scale. We were walking for about four hours, and the streets were packed with people on multiple blocks and intersections. There were moments where we couldn’t even move because of the sheer amount of people. There were dozens of different groups and contingents out there, bands playing songs, and chants filling the streets with so much energy. A majority of people there came from different walks of life. The general strike reflected France’s multinational and multigenerational population. It wasn’t just students out there. Talking to the people on the ground—the students, the elders, the mothers, the labor union members—they all expressed concerns around the economic and material conditions in France becoming more detrimental to everyday people as the year has progressed. People mentioned issues with wages, their ability to attend college, access to healthcare, and affording housing and food with rising inflation costs in France. They were telling us that the state of the education system reflects the larger economic issues within the French system. We also saw people on the street tying these economic issues to war and imperialism and the severe state violence and racism against Black, Arab, and Muslim people in France. Even though the media may try to paint it as though people are protesting against Macron and just the government, on the ground, people said these issues aren’t just created by Macron and his government. They were quite literally naming capitalism as the issue and fighting for a new system where people are placed above profit. It was truly inspiring to be on the ground and hear people naming that clearly. Even when we were there on November 5th, there was a perception of, “Oh, what’s going to happen? Is this going to be the end of the movement?” But no, talking to people on the ground, they were energized and determined to continue taking to the streets. As you mentioned, Zoe, they have plans for the weeks ahead to continue blockading their schools. Even this week, many universities and high schools are continuing to be blockaded. Dozens of political groups and unions are pushing for other mass shutdowns in the coming month. It was very clear, talking to people on the ground, that they believe it’s people power that transforms society. The main demonstration in Paris was in an important site in the history of the French Revolution. People in the streets are well aware of that history and know the history of France’s revolutionary past and the history of former colonies of France as well. Many people in the streets come from second and third-generation immigrant families from former French colonies like Algeria and many other African countries. They know that it’s people organizing and taking to the streets that makes change inevitable and will build a new system for them. [Speaker 1:] I’m so happy you mentioned that because it segues perfectly into our next question. We’ve been watching the coverage of the protests in France and covering it here on Break Through News over the last month. Something that’s really animated those protests is the omnipresence of Palestinian flags and keffiyehs. We know these are symbols of Palestine, but they’ve also become symbols synonymous with resistance for movements around the world. We also know that these protests in France have been led by Black and Arab youth from the suburbs of Paris, who are the children and grandchildren of people from parts of the world that France colonized. Talk to us about the connection with the movement against genocide, the struggle of Black and Arab youth in France against racism and Islamophobia, and how that’s all connected in this movement against war and austerity that you’ve been witnessing today. [Iman D:] For myself, being a student organizer for Palestine, I was in awe of the sheer number of keffiyehs, Palestine flags, signs, and banners standing in solidarity for Palestine during the general strike and other demonstrations we attended that week. I got goosebumps seeing people on the streets during the general strike chanting “Free, free Palestine” and connecting all these struggles. When I talked to the students and different people in the anti-imperialist contingents on the ground, many people made the point that Palestine opened up their consciousness. It made them think about the French government and its capacity to commit and aid in genocide, the inflated war budget, while they’re sitting in classrooms with no seats, crumbling walls, no heating, and no plumbing in cold weather conditions. Each time we asked students and youth where the government money is going, they always mentioned war and genocide. For many of these people, a free Palestine means having a better world where they don’t have to experience the racism and abuse they face under the system in France. You brought up the working-class Arab and Black youth. It was them that truly paved the movement we see in France. It started in the suburbs, led by Arab and Black youth. For many of them, they talked about seeing this struggle in France and seeing themselves with the struggle for Palestine. Palestine changed their minds and built this level of consciousness for them, and they were aware that the same system investing millions and trillions in dehumanizing and killing Palestinians is the same system in France investing over 34 billion euros annually in the police system to dehumanize them in their neighborhoods and kill Black and Arab youth every day. The youth described police violence and terrorism against Black and Arab neighborhoods as continued colonialism. They tied this to the fact that cops in France train with the IDF, which is nothing new, coming from America knowing this. These police forces originate from colonial police forces that brutalized their grandparents and killed people in Algeria, North, and West Africa in the 20th century under French occupation. They were well aware that for them, there is no choosing one cause over another or abandoning one cause for another. There’s no sacrificing their language to appeal to a broader audience. These kids were speaking more to international solidarity than their local politicians and anyone else. It was truly inspiring to see and hear that. We also had the opportunity to go to Saint-Denis, a suburb in Paris with a historically Arab, Black, and Muslim working-class majority. We visited the high school there and heard from students about the systemic Islamophobia and racism they witness every day. They talked about the 2004 French law prohibiting wearing any religious symbols to schools and shared stories about having their hoodies pulled down at school if they covered their hair. We even witnessed Muslim girls having to remove their hijab before entering school and the trauma of enduring that every day. Additionally, students shared stories of cops coming into their classrooms and abducting their peers. They showed us videos of that happening and described how cops randomly bag check them in their cities, follow them around, and how one wrong look at a cop can lead to a life or death incident. They said their neighborhoods are literally occupied by militarized police forces. I myself can attest to experiencing police intimidation during my week there. We were stopped multiple times entering and leaving protests, doing bag checks. Our group was circled by cops and forced to do random bag checks, and they even claimed my sister and I had false passports. Witnessing that and hearing those stories and experiences, these youth are well aware that the struggle against state violence they experience in France is the same as the struggle against the war forces that France is investing in. In the US, we see many similarities. Youth across the nation have become conscious and have continued to tie their struggles to the fact that the US war machine is the largest investor in the genocide of Palestinians in the world. College students in the US question why they are drowning in college debt and healthcare debt, not even being guaranteed a job after graduation with the state of the economy, while the country continues to invest trillions in war and the war machine. People have tied their struggle against the war machine to police violence and brutality. The NYPD and LAPD are trained by the IDF. Black people are brutalized and murdered by cops across the nation daily. Our struggles against state violence from France to the United States to Palestine are all one struggle against the same system, which is capitalism. The people of France truly understand that their fight against racism, anti-Blackness, anti-Muslim fascism, and state violence is tied to Palestine. They’re aware that the same system funding the war in the streets of France against Black and Arab youth is the same system funding genocide and imperialism abroad. They see and understand their struggle as one. They’re asking why, in the same way that in the US, we’re asking why our system is investing billions and trillions in police and war abroad and then cutting social services, telling us we can’t afford healthcare for all or housing because we don’t have enough money. The math is not adding up, and people in France and the US know that. [Speaker 1:] Iman, you gave me chills describing those scenes. That is extremely powerful. You are not only Algerian, but you are also Minnesotan. You were on the streets of the Twin Cities for the historic general strikes on January 23rd and January 30th. What was it like having lived through and organized for the Minnesota general strikes and then to see one play out in France? What similarities did you draw, and what lessons do you take from both of these experiences as people across the world face growing inequality, declining living standards, and a seemingly endless desire from the ruling class to wage war and enrich themselves? [Iman D:] As we know, in December 2023, Operation Metro Surge began in Minnesota, where over 2,000 ICE agents were deployed to the Twin Cities to carry out one of the largest DHS operations ever in history. During their time there, we witnessed the arrest and abduction of over 3,000 people. Importantly, we saw the extent of violence that state and federal agents were willing to go to, including the murder of Renee Good and Alex Kueng. After the murder of Renee Good on January 7th, the people of Minnesota refused to back down. They were like, “Enough is enough.” We saw unions, political organizations, student organizations, and even some local officials join the call for a general strike on January 23rd to fight against this. Similarly to the people in France, the masses of Minnesota knew that the occupation of federal agents in their city and these agents killing their neighbors wouldn’t end by complying with Trump. They also knew that public officials like the Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey or former governor Tim Walz weren’t going to do anything about it, quite transparently, the same way that in France they knew public officials aren’t going to change their conditions. In Minnesota, especially from the memory of 2020 after the murder of George Floyd and millions taking to the streets across the nation to demand change, Minnesotans knew this time again that it takes organization and people taking to the streets to create that change. On January 23rd, we saw this historic general strike where over 100,000 Minnesotans from all walks of life, similarly to France, took to the streets in negative 20° weather. That’s one difference. [laughter] They made it clear who holds power in our system. They knew it’s not Trump, DHS, millionaires, or billionaires. It’s people. It’s working people that hold power. Like France, people are well aware that it’s people that transform society collectively if we take serious organizing and show up in unity. That was such a historic moment. The day after January 23rd, one of the largest general strikes in Minnesota’s history, we witnessed the murder of Alex Kueng in the streets of Minneapolis. It was very clear the message that the federal government was trying to send, which is either comply or be killed. Like the people in France who have been protesting for over six weeks now, the people of Minnesota knew they wouldn’t just back down after this incident. After the murder, I was out on the block where Alex Kueng was murdered because a bunch of people had gathered there. We heard folks chanting “strike, strike, strike” on the ground. I remember people telling me we need to extend the strike to be a week-long strike. I heard people demanding more than that, demanding a whole new system, very similarly to what I was hearing in France where people were saying it’s not just this one issue, it’s the whole system that’s the issue. People were done with state violence and the system that passively allows for this. Seeing all these similarities was very clear with people knowing it’s only themselves that can change their conditions, not one local or political figure. The next day after January 24th, who made the call for the January 30th shutdown? It was Black and Somali students at the University of Minnesota, and the shutdown spread across the nation. In France, the call was made by Black and Arab students in the suburbs. Honestly, being on the ground in France last week, witnessing the general strike brought me to tears. It gave me a lot of revolutionary optimism to see the people power on the ground. Knowing the history of Minnesota and people power there, we can’t let anyone forget about that. They want us to forget about this history. They want us to forget about the history in the US of different movements where it’s people power that made change, like the civil rights movement, like the 2006 Day of Immigration. Seeing all of that together makes me think about how we really have to hold on to our history, remember our history of resistance in the US, and seeing that power in the streets of France brings me optimism. In Minnesota, we saw that it wasn’t like the ICE operation ended and Tom Homan was kicked out because of public officials. It was people taking to the streets and staying on the streets until real change happened. They didn’t do it willingly. They were left with no choice but to end the operation. [Speaker 1:] I want to ask you lastly, given, as I’m sure you saw, people in the US ushered in this crushing blow to Donald Trump in last Tuesday’s midterm elections. We saw this unprecedented blue tsunami, but people were voting overwhelmingly not necessarily for the Democrats, but actually against Trump’s party, his MAGA movement, to register their rejection of many things, including the illegal criminal war of aggression on Iran, their anger about the escalation, the attacks from ICE on immigrant communities, the economic and cost of living crises, many of which are directly resulting from the Iran war, opposition to the genocide in Gaza, which ironically the Democrats also participated in. But all that’s to say, you’ve been on the ground seeing this movement energy. You saw this movement energy in Minnesota. Now that we’ve seen the MAGA movement really collapse since these midterms, as somebody who’s an organizer and who’s in movement building, what do you think comes next in this moment with regard to the US? [Iman D:] When we were on the ground in France, each time we told people we were American, a lot of people asked us immediately about our thoughts on the midterms. [laughter] We reciprocated that question back, asking their thoughts on the US midterms. Many people talked about the midterms in the US and this blue tsunami giving them a sense of optimism against the MAGA movement and this right-wing agenda more than in support directly of the Democratic Party. They connected that with their upcoming presidential election in April 2027, talking about these right-wing forces and Macron needing to be out of office. But they also highlighted the importance of continuing to take to the streets regardless of the results in April 2027. We can acknowledge last Tuesday was a blow to the MAGA movement and the right-wing agenda, showing a clear shift in American public opinion and voting for progressive politicians. It’s clear people are looking for change. But again, talking to the people in France, a lesson we’re familiar with and can bring to the US is that we know it’s mass movements that create change. Now that we see the shift, our task is to hold public officials accountable and push for more, like the people in France. We know that ICE and police violence will continue. The war on Iran is still looming. Rent prices will continue to spike. More and more people will continue to drown in student and healthcare debt. It’s important to remember the power we have as people. Even thinking back to Minnesota, we had Democratic officials in office in the state, and they didn’t do anything to push out ICE. It was people power that did that. As we’re seeing these crises unfold, climate change continuing to detriment our neighborhoods and communities, war escalating with Iran, ICE terror continuing in our communities, and AI backed by billionaires leaving more young adults jobless and unemployed, it’s clear we can’t just depend on the Democratic Party or public officials to change our system. We’re going to need to take to the streets like France to organize and build towards a mass movement demanding a whole change in our system. We know our conditions won’t change unless we do that, and we can learn that through the history of the US, through January, and through the protest movements happening in France. We just have to remind ourselves of that history and continue to organize and build towards a new system. [Speaker 1:] Iman, you have really radiated that revolutionary optimism. I’m feeling pumped. I know we have to go through the laborious task of talking about what’s happened on Capitol Hill since these midterm results, but I think that point is well taken. It will be the mass movement that decides the future and what policies will get implemented, what policies will get passed. Very important lessons to take there. Iman D, student organizer, we thank you so much for joining us here on BT Live and bringing that very vivid recap of your time in Paris because it sounds like you witnessed history. Really powerful stuff there. [Iman D:] Yes, thank you, Zoe and Rania. It was great being able to discuss with you all today.

articles.title: General strike brings Spain to a halt
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Hundreds of thousands of workers in key sectors – with total participation likely in the millions – responded to a general strike call in Spain on Wednesday, November 11, demanding solutions to the housing crisis and protection of labor rights. The action represents the first nationwide work stoppage in 14 years. The strike was called by the country’s largest trade unions – the General Union of Workers (Unión General de Trabajadores, UGT) and the Workers’ Commissions (Comisiones Obreras) – alongside tenants associations and other unions, including the General Confederation of Labor (Confederación General del Trabajo, CGT). Read more: 1.6 million join general strike in France against austerity “More than 2,500 picket lines across the country are out informing people about the reasons for the strike – a mobilization for the right to housing and for wage increases that is both massive and unprecedented in our history,” the CGT stated on the day. “This day of action is mobilizing thousands of people across the country with one clear goal: to demand solutions on housing and wages,” added CGT General Secretary Miguel Fadrique. “As unions, we must heed this message and keep up the fight.” Broad response to the strike call The UGT and Comisiones Obreras reported that early data indicated a 90% strike adherence in the automotive sector, followed by industrial action in the meat industry and waste collection at 85% and 82%, as well as 75% in the energy sector. “The response in the ports of Algeciras and Valencia is also notable, with participation reaching 90%,” the unions wrote. Overall adherence varied by region. Unions reported figures ranging from 41% in Castilla-La Mancha and Extremadura to over 80% in Catalonia and Andalusia. This translated into disruptions of public transport and air traffic around Barcelona, as well as a full halt at the SEAT factory in the region, unions emphasized . Media workers joined the strike as well, with broadcasts on some public television stations going dark. Additionally, the UGT and Comisiones Obreras pointed out that “one significant effect of the strike was a reduction in electricity consumption of more than 10% – a sharper decline than during previous general strikes.” The decrease in electricity consumption is being read as another sign of strong strike adherence, suggesting that significantly fewer people are adhering to their usual schedules. Trade unions denounced police repression and violence, including the use of tear gas, against picketers. Source: UGT/X On the other hand, trade unions denounced attempts to obstruct the strike and police repression against picket lines. They reported the use of pepper spray against protesters in Madrid, as well as several arrests and attacks against pickets blocking roads and building entrances. Unions also criticized regional governments – especially in Madrid – for imposing minimum service requirements at a level that effectively curtailed the right to strike. The UGT and Comisiones Obreras linked these decisions to a somewhat lower strike adherence in sectors including post services and healthcare – but insisted this did not diminish the overall success of the strike. A historic alliance with tenant associations The nationwide industrial action is taking place three weeks ahead of a snap election called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez after parliament failed to pass emergency housing bills last month. The legislation was drafted after the eviction – and later death – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal triggered massive demonstrations and encampments denouncing the commodification of housing and real estate speculation in Spain. The protests pushed trade unions to issue the first general strike call since 2012, connecting housing grievances to the broader cost-of-living crisis. “The housing situation has become a catalyst for the discontent that cuts across Spanish society,” wrote Comisiones Obreras General Secretary Unai Sordo . “An increasing number of individuals and families find themselves choked by the burden of unaffordable mortgage or rent payments – or are even unable to lead an independent life.” Read more: Housing crisis leads to snap election in Spain In addition to labor unions, the November 11 general strike was co-launched with tenant associations, ushering in a collaboration of historic importance. “We’ve proven we can organize on a scale no one thought possible,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union (Sindicato de Inquilinas e Inquilinos de Madrid) wrote on the eve of the strike. “We’ve built alliances that until very recently seemed unthinkable. We’ve made an entire country talk about housing – using our terminology and our images.” “We have lost our fear. And no one can take that away from us now. Not a struck-down decree, not a vulture fund, not a hostile headline.”

articles.title: Outrage and anger in Paraguay: a new president is sworn in, but there is no relief
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Although many had hoped Santiago Peña’s resignation as president of Paraguay would calm the anger of millions of Paraguayans, it did not. As the hours pass, hundreds of protesters are joining spontaneous demonstrations against Paraguay’s political and economic establishment. And the truth is, this comes as no surprise. It has been revealed that Ueno Bank was a financial institution that grew rapidly thanks to contributions from pensioners and other state-linked sources that Peña’s own government ordered to be injected into a bank that had only just been officially recognized as such in 2023. Privatization becomes national scam But what has outraged millions of Paraguayans the most is that, according to several judicial investigations, Ueno’s own shareholders were taking the money coming in from the government and lending it to companies linked to themselves. And this perverse cycle of Paraguayan taxpayers’ money being used so cynically by private individuals appears to have been orchestrated by several people, including former President Peña himself – or at least that is what the prosecution alleges. As a result, a judge ordered Peña’s pretrial detention at a military barrack, where he will be allowed to receive visitors and use his phone – a development that has further inflamed the anger of thousands of Paraguayans demanding their money back and justice. When a young Paraguayan woman was asked if she had been affected by the Ueno case, she said something that perfectly captures the sentiment of millions: “Of course, it affects me and everyone else. The money they’re using to reimburse us comes from all the public banks. That means that Ueno customers had their money stolen, and those who don’t have [accounts at Ueno] also had their money stolen, because the money they’re using to reimburse us comes from everyone. They’re stealing to replace what was stolen.” The prosecution alleges that the right-wing former president of the long-standing Colorado Party committed breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain through his dealings with a bank owned by a business group in which Peña himself had invested in previous years. Furthermore, Peña appointed Carvallo, the former president of Ueno, to head the Central Bank, a move that has also led to the opening of a criminal investigation against Carvallo. The Colorado Party and neoliberal economics For its part, the ruling Colorado Party has attempted to distance itself from its member Peña, hoping that its image will not be so severely compromised. Former President Cartes even quickly called for Peña’s removal. In his place, former Vice President Pedro Alliana assumed the presidency; in an attempt to gain some legitimacy, he has called for the resignation of all ministers appointed by Peña. However, several analysts perceive in the streets of Paraguay not only great disappointment with the political system (which is largely controlled by the Colorado Party and Paraguay’s major neoliberal business leaders) but also a great deal of anger and frustration among the population, especially among younger people. “They’re all the same – everyone in the Colorado [Party] is a bunch of hypocrites, rats, who stick together and ask God to bless Paraguay. But God will bless Paraguay when all of you go to hell,” the same protester declared , while the interviewer noted that other young people had told him on the streets of Asunción that they feel completely let down and disappointed. Possible change? However, it remains to be seen whether such disappointment and anger can translate into a political and economic alternative for Paraguay, a country that was controlled for much of the 20th century by the US-backed dictator Alfredo Stroessner (1954–1989), who led one of the harshest and longest-lasting dictatorships of the century through force and electoral fraud. Stroessner had been a member of the Colorado Party since 1951 and was one of the key figures in Operation Condor, in which other military governments acted in concert to repress, assassinate, rape, and disappear the region’s progressive and revolutionary forces. And although he was overthrown in a military coup, the party that supported him the most – the Colorado Party – continued to dominate Paraguayan politics for most of the 21st century, except for the brief presidency (overturned by the old Paraguayan powers) of the progressive Fernando Lugo. For now, it remains to be seen whether the Colorado Party will manage to save itself once again as Paraguay’s main (and virtually sole) hegemonic political force, or whether a new political alternative might emerge from the ashes of the biggest economic scandal in Paraguay’s contemporary history (and one of the most traumatic in the region) although, unfortunately, this is by no means the only story of the rich and powerful shamelessly exploiting the state for their own gain. There are still vivid examples of this in Latin America: Paraguay seems to be just one more case, though perhaps it could become the case that opens the eyes of more than a few, and that is why so many are keeping a close watch on its streets.

articles.title: “American Scoundrel”: From Roy Cohn to Stephen Miller, “McCarthyism Lives On,” Says Author Kai Bird
articles.content: We speak with historian Kai Bird about American Scoundrel , a new biography of the notorious political fixer Roy Cohn, who rose to fame as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy during the senator’s anti-communist campaign, served as a lawyer for the New York mob, and was an influential voice in Republican circles until his death from AIDS -related complications in 1986. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s. Facing political setbacks during his first term as president, Trump reportedly asked, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Bird, who co-authored American Scoundrel with his wife Susan Goldmark, says Trump may have found his Cohn in Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation policies whom Trump just elevated to chief of staff. “It’s not really a surprise that, cornered and wounded by the recent election results, he reaches out and pulls up Stephen Miller, who’s very similar in his willingness to go on the offensive and never back down, and to say outrageous things to try to change the narrative,” says Bird.

articles.title: Meet David Morales: Providence Voters Elect Democratic Socialist Mayor, Approve Israel Divestment
articles.content: Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence. “What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. And for that reason, we are seeing a rise in democratic socialism and the representation of democratic socialists all across the country.”

articles.title: “Birds of War”: New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
articles.content: We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary Birds of War , which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC , and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence. The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions. “Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.” Birds of War premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

articles.title: Yet another catastrophic winter in Gaza
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: For the fourth consecutive year, and more than a year after the US-brokered ceasefire deal was reached, Palestinian people in Gaza continue to suffer from a severe humanitarian crisis caused by extreme weather conditions amid ongoing Israeli assaults and restrictions. On Sunday, November 8, a steep sand dune collapsed onto tents sheltering displaced people in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip, killing five people , including four children and a woman. A number of other injured people were rescued from the site, according to media reports. A report issued by the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF) on Monday, November 9, revealed that the catastrophic weather conditions have affected over 106,000 people in the besieged enclave. Seasonal storms have flooded at least 70,000 tents, while 22,000 others collapsed completely, as Israel continues to restrict and delay the entry of essential shelter supplies, heating equipment, repair machinery, and maintenance parts to the war-ravaged territory. Heavy rainfall also overwhelmed Gaza’s already damaged water and sewage infrastructure, resulting in widespread flooding of raw sewage across displacement camps. Moreover, the sudden drop in overnight temperatures below 10°C (50°F) triggers life-threatening risk, particularly for children and sick people, especially with the shortage of winter clothes, blankets, and heating fuel. International organizations hold Israel accountable for exacerbating the impact of severe weather conditions The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor accused the Israeli government of subjecting “Palestinians’ right to shelter and recovery to Israeli electoral calculations, particularly amid reports that measures to reconstruct Gaza have been postponed until after the elections.” “Electoral interests and political or military conditions cannot justify suspending civilian protection or depriving people of life’s necessities,” the Geneva-based organization noted. It also blamed international measures for falling short “to stop these practices and hold those responsible accountable,” which the organization said “has allowed Israel to continue using such deprivation as leverage, without facing a deterrent cost.” Meanwhile, Regional Director for the Middle East, North Africa and Eastern Europe at Save the Children International, Ahmad Alhendawi, criticized the US-brokered ceasefire for failing “to protect Palestinian children.” “This is not simply the result of bad weather. Tents, shelter kits, and fuel are waiting at Gaza’s borders while children sleep in floodwater, because the Israeli authorities are blocking their entry. This is a choice, and children are paying the price. More than a year into the so-called ceasefire, it has failed to protect Palestinian children,” Alhendawi stated.

articles.title: La crisis financiera y política en Paraguay: una muestra más del fracaso del modelo económico liberal
articles.author: Thania Saucedo
articles.content: Read in English here Paraguay atraviesa una de las crisis políticas y financieras más importantes de su historia reciente. La intervención de Ueno Bank por parte del Banco Central del Paraguay, luego de detectarse graves irregularidades en sus operaciones y problemas de solvencia, desató una crisis que rápidamente dejó de ser solamente bancaria. Hoy tiene consecuencias directas sobre el Gobierno de Santiago Peña y abrió un proceso de juicio político que pone en cuestión la continuidad del propio presidente de la República. Para entender lo que está pasando es necesario explicar algunos elementos. Ueno Bank experimentó un crecimiento exponencial en los últimos años, coincidiendo con el inicio del Gobierno de Santiago Peña. Llegó a tener cerca de tres millones de clientes, más del 50% de la población adulta del país, y recibió alrededor de 800 millones de dólares en depósitos del sector público. Entre esos recursos se encuentran fondos vinculados al Instituto de Previsión Social (IPS), que administra los aportes jubilatorios y de salud de miles de trabajadoras y trabajadores. Uno de los problemas es que el propio presidente de la República mantuvo vínculos empresariales con el grupo relacionado con la entidad bancaria hasta marzo de 2025. A esto se suma que Carlos Carvallo, quien había presidido Financiera Ueno, pasó posteriormente a dirigir el Banco Central, organismo responsable de supervisar y controlar al sistema financiero. Durante este Gobierno también se modificaron las disposiciones que buscaban impedir este tipo de conflictos de intereses, conocidas como normativa de puerta giratoria. La intervención del banco, la inmovilización de los depósitos y las investigaciones sobre créditos concedidos a empresas vinculadas a sus propietarios terminaron exponiendo una trama de relaciones entre intereses privados y las instituciones públicas. Sin embargo, además, detrás de las cifras y de las operaciones financieras, hay miles de personas que hoy no pueden disponer de sus ahorros; trabajadores que enfrentan incertidumbre sobre sus salarios y jubilados cuyos recursos están comprometidos. La inclusión financiera, que se presentó como uno de los grandes logros del modelo económico, terminó convirtiéndose en una enorme estafa para la población. Los vínculos de Santiago Peña con el grupo empresarial, las decisiones adoptadas desde el Ejecutivo y las responsabilidades de los organismos de control forman parte de los cuestionamientos que dieron origen al pedido de juicio político. La oposición impulsó el proceso en el Congreso y el 5 de noviembre la Cámara de Diputados aprobó la acusación contra el mandatario. Peña presentó su renuncia, pero ambas cámaras rechazaron esa salida y el Senado continuó con el proceso. Al momento de escribir estas líneas, el presidente debe ejercer su defensa ante el juicio político. Sin embargo, para entender esta crisis hay que mirar también hacia la Asociación Nacional Republicana (ANR), el Partido Colorado, – profundamente ligada a la estructura del Estado paraguayo y a los 35 años de dictadura de Alfredo Stroessner – y particularmente hacia Horacio Cartes (HC). Paraguay tiene una particularidad política que resulta fundamental para comprender lo que sucede. El Partido Colorado gobierna prácticamente de manera ininterrumpida desde 1947, la única interrupción de ese largo ciclo fue el gobierno de Fernando Lugo (2008-2012), que llegó al poder encabezando una alianza que logró derrotar electoralmente al coloradismo después de más de seis décadas. Sin embargo, su Gobierno terminó abruptamente en junio de 2012, mediante un golpe parlamentario que en apenas 48 horas lo destituyó a través de un cuestionado juicio político. Para los movimientos sociales y sectores del campo popular, ese hecho no fue un episodio más en la historia sino una operación política articulada por sectores de la derecha paraguaya, con Horacio Cartes como uno de sus principales actores y con presuntas complicidades y respaldo de intereses externos, entre ellos los de la Embajada de los Estados Unidos. En la actualidad, el poder dentro de la ANR está fuertemente disputado por sus movimientos internos, pero el cartismo (HC), se convirtió en el principal espacio de poder del oficialismo. Cartes no solamente fue presidente de la República entre 2013 y 2018, sino que posteriormente asumió la presidencia del propio Partido Colorado y mantuvo una enorme influencia sobre las decisiones del Gobierno de Santiago Peña. Peña llegó a la Presidencia impulsado políticamente por Cartes. Su candidatura y posterior gobierno se construyeron bajo el liderazgo del movimiento Honor Colorado. Por eso, lo que estamos viendo hoy tiene una contradicción política muy importante; el mismo sector que construyó y sostuvo este gobierno ahora decide acompañar el juicio político contra el presidente. La posición de Cartes fue cambiando a medida que avanzaba la crisis. Inicialmente, desde su entorno se rechazaba la posibilidad de un juicio político y se buscaba concentrar la responsabilidad en las autoridades del Banco Central. Sin embargo, el 5 de noviembre, Cartes anunció públicamente que la ANR acompañaría el enjuiciamiento de Peña. Este movimiento no puede leerse simplemente como una decisión institucional del Partido Colorado, también expresa una disputa por el control político, por la continuidad del proyecto de gobierno y por la preservación de un esquema de poder que el propio movimiento contribuyó a construir. A partir de este escenario, desde los movimientos sociales y el campo popular, la denuncia no se limita a exigir responsabilidades individuales y rechazar cualquier intento de impunidad, también advierte que esta crisis es una muestra más del fracaso del modelo económico liberal que, durante años repitió que el mercado podía regularse por sí mismo, que el Estado debía reducir su intervención y que la privatización y la desregulación eran el camino para alcanzar el desarrollo. Prometieron que, si dejábamos funcionar libremente al capital, la riqueza terminaría llegando a toda la población y que el crecimiento económico se traduciría en bienestar y que todas y todos se beneficiarían de ese supuesto derrame. En Paraguay, hoy las consecuencias están sobre la mesa de cada trabajador, producto del narco capitalismo financiero. Un modelo que administra de manera inescrupulosa los recursos públicos, concentra riquezas y establece relaciones entre el poder político y los intereses privados. Un sistema en el que las ganancias quedan en manos de determinados sectores, mientras las consecuencias de sus operaciones terminan recayendo sobre la población. Por tanto, lo que ocurre en este lado del sur de nuestra América, no está ajeno a lo que sucede en otras partes del mundo, es parte de una dinámica en la que los grandes capitales condicionan las decisiones políticas, se apropian de los bienes comunes y convierten derechos y necesidades básicas en oportunidades de negocio. Cambian los escenarios, cambian los actores, pero la lógica sigue siendo la misma. Sin embargo, el evidente fracaso de la política económica del capitalismo financiero también abre una oportunidad para el campo popular organizado: disputar otro horizonte y construir una alternativa política y económica que rompa con esta lógica. De abrir camino hacia un mundo en el que la economía esté al servicio de la vida y no de la acumulación de unos pocos y en el que los pueblos puedan decidir sobre sus recursos, su presente y su destino. Thania Saucedo es comunicadora y dirigente política por el Frente Guasu, Paraguay. Este artículo fue producido por Globetrotter .

articles.title: La India en el Mediterráneo
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: Read in English here El 26 de octubre de 2026, el ministro de Relaciones Exteriores de Grecia, George Gerapetritis, se presentó en la sede de las Naciones Unidas y rechazó el acuerdo marítimo entre Turquía y Libia. Gerapetritis habló en nombre de Grecia, por supuesto, pero también de Bahrein, Chipre, Egipto, la Unión Europea y los Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Cinco días después, la fragata india INS Trishul ingresó a la bahía de Souda, en Creta, como parte de actividades con la instalación de la Armada de los Estados Unidos (Actividad de Apoyo Naval) y con el Centro de Entrenamiento Operativo de Interdicción Marítima de la OTAN. Esta secuencia pone de manifiesto una geografía estratégica en desarrollo: el alcance naval de la India, su confrontación con el nuevo socio turco de Pakistán y su ambición de conectar el capital indio con los mercados europeos convergen cada vez más en el Mediterráneo oriental. Campos energéticos El 20 de octubre, el Gobierno de Acuerdo Nacional de Libia, con sede en Bengasi, aprobó un memorando marítimo firmado con Turquía en 2019. Grecia, que mantiene una relación hostil con Turquía, argumenta que la delimitación establecida en el memorando ignora los derechos marítimos de las islas que Grecia reclama, como Creta; la Unión Europea (UE), coincidiendo con Grecia, argumenta que este memorando infringe los derechos de terceros Estados. Por supuesto, Turquía acogió con satisfacción la decisión de Bengasi y rechazó la declaración de la UE. Estos argumentos se ven agravados por el petróleo que yace bajo las olas. En febrero, Chevron y Helleniq Energy firmaron un acuerdo para explorar cuatro bloques petroleros marítimos griegos, incluidos dos al sur de Creta. Chevron tiene una participación operativa del 70% en este proyecto, que prevé la exploración sísmica de yacimientos potenciales. Las concesiones demuestran por qué son importantes las fronteras marítimas, ya que los mapas en conflicto pueden tener un impacto enorme en futuros descubrimientos de petróleo. La odisea de la India En agosto de 2023, el primer ministro de la India, Narendra Modi, viajó a Atenas y se reunió con el primer ministro griego, Kyriakos Mitsotakis. Firmaron un acuerdo que reforzó la Asociación de Conectividad entre la India y la UE de mayo de 2021, la cual, en apariencia, abarca una amplia gama de temas, pero que, en el fondo, se centra principalmente en acuerdos para grandes corporaciones relacionados con puertos, cables submarinos y redes satelitales. En febrero de 2024, Modi y Mitsotakis vincularon explícitamente la cooperación en el Mediterráneo oriental con los objetivos bélicos de los Estados Unidos en Asia, al referirse – en la versión griega – a “un mar Mediterráneo y un Indo-Pacífico libres, abiertos y basados en normas” (Modi le dijo a Mitsotakis que “es motivo de alegría que Grecia haya decidido sumarse a la Iniciativa de los Océanos Indo-Pacíficos”, una plataforma impulsada por la India para la cooperación científica, pero principalmente para la seguridad marítima). Desde entonces, la relación institucional se ha profundizado con una Declaración Conjunta de Intenciones de febrero de 2026 sobre cooperación industrial en materia de defensa y, posteriormente, con un Plan de Cooperación Militar Bilateral. El secretario de Defensa de la India, Rajesh Kumar Singh, visitó Chipre y Grecia a mediados de octubre para dar seguimiento a la Asociación de Seguridad y Defensa entre la India y la UE . A medida que la India y Grecia cerraban estos acuerdos diplomáticos y militares, los buques de la Armada india llegaron uno tras otro a Grecia. Antes del INS Trishul , el INS Tamal hizo escala en la Bahía de Souda en agosto de 2025, mientras que el INS Trikand llegó a Salamina en septiembre de 2025 y participó en el primer ejercicio naval entre la India y Grecia. ¿Por qué la India de Modi está tan interesada en este acuerdo con Grecia? Además de lo que dice el texto, cabe mencionar otras dos cuestiones contextuales: en primer lugar, los acuerdos comerciales impulsados por el principal patrocinador corporativo de Modi, Gautam Adani, y, en segundo lugar, los acuerdos emergentes en materia de seguridad en Asia Occidental desarrollados por Pakistán, Turquía y Arabia Saudita. Los puertos de Adani En 2022, Adani Ports, de Gautam Adani, formó una empresa conjunta con la firma israelí Gadot para adquirir el puerto de Haifa en Israel, en la que Adani tiene una participación del 70%. Esta adquisición le permitió a Adani establecer una posición sólida en una puerta de entrada al Mediterráneo. Menos de un año después, en septiembre de 2023, en la cumbre del G20 celebrada en Nueva Delhi, varios países, como la India y los Estados Unidos, se unieron a la Unión Europea para anunciar la creación de un Corredor Económico India-Oriente Medio-Europa ( IMEC ). El proceso del IMEC forma parte del esfuerzo respaldado por los Estados Unidos para ofrecer una alternativa a la Iniciativa de la Franja y la Ruta liderada por China. La ruta es sencilla: comienza en Gujarat y Maharashtra, se dirige al Golfo por barco, se conecta con las redes ferroviarias a través de Arabia Saudita, Jordania e Israel, y luego, desde Israel, se dirige a Grecia y Francia. Lo que llama la atención es que a lo largo de todo el recorrido del IMEC se encuentran propiedades que pertenecen a diversas corporaciones de Adani: desde los puertos de Kandla y Mundra (en Gujarat, India) hasta Haifa (Israel) y luego a Marsella (con el continuo intento de adquirir participaciones en puertos griegos). En cierto sentido, el IMEC es menos una red de naciones y más una cadena global de puertos propiedad de Adani. El itinerario propuesto por el IMEC elude deliberadamente a Turquía, dando prioridad a una conexión entre el Golfo, Israel y Europa que sirve a la agenda de integración regional de Washington, al tiempo que limita el papel de Ankara como potencia de tránsito. El presidente de los EE. UU., Joe Biden, lo presentó explícitamente como una contribución a un Oriente Medio económicamente integrado que convirtiera a Israel en el punto de tránsito del Mediterráneo en lugar de a Turquía. La lógica de esta ruta debe entenderse a la luz de los Acuerdos de Abraham , diseñados por los Estados Unidos para impulsar a diversos Estados árabes a normalizar formalmente sus relaciones con Israel. El IMEC, al instar a Arabia Saudita a permitir que las rutas comerciales atravesaran Israel, habría terminado siendo, de facto, un ejercicio de normalización. La necesidad de evitar Turquía y pasar por Israel no tenía que ver con el comercio, sino que, para los Estados Unidos, se trataba exclusivamente de la política de normalización a favor de Israel. El Acuerdo de La Meca El ataque estadounidense-israelí contra Irán cambió por completo el paradigma de seguridad en Asia Occidental. La represalia de Irán contra las bases militares estadounidenses en los Estados árabes del Golfo transmitió el mensaje de que los Estados Unidos no puede ser un escudo de defensa adecuado para estas regiones. La opinión generalizada es ahora que los países de Asia Occidental deben unirse para buscar su seguridad a través de negociaciones. El 7 de agosto de 2026, Pakistán, Arabia Saudita y Turquía firmaron un acuerdo de defensa conjunta que consideraba un ataque armado contra uno de ellos como un ataque contra los tres. Antes de ese anuncio, Asim Munir, de Pakistán, viajó a Teherán para informar a los líderes iraníes de que el acuerdo de La Meca no estaba diseñado en contra de Irán, sino para crear una plataforma que no incluyera a los Estados Unidos (y, para octubre, los ministros de Defensa de los tres países viajaron a Irán para calmar cualquier tensión). El 11 de agosto, funcionarios de la India declararon que estaban monitoreando la situación, y más adelante ese mismo mes, cuando Bangladés indicó que estaba considerando unirse al acuerdo, la India reiteró una vez más que mantenía un ojo en el acuerdo. De todo esto, se ha escrito poco sobre la creciente relación de Pakistán con Turquía. En febrero de 2025, Ankara e Islamabad firmaron acuerdos que abarcaban la cooperación en guerra electrónica, los intercambios de personal militar y la capacitación en salud militar. Tres meses después, en mayo, la India y Pakistán libraron una guerra aérea en la que Pakistán utilizó drones YIHA-III y Asisguard Songar de origen turco (con una controversia adicional, negada por Ankara, de que seis aeronaves militares turcas aterrizaron en Pakistán a finales de abril). El 22 de septiembre de 2026, el presidente Recep Tayyip Erdoğan planteó el tema de Cachemira ante la Asamblea General de la ONU, lo cual la India rechazó una semana después. El acercamiento de la India a Grecia, que tiene sus propios conflictos con Turquía respecto a Chipre, le ofrece a Delhi una influencia potencial en la región vecina de Turquía. El equilibrio de Arabia Saudita entre su cercanía con los Estados Unidos y su deseo de ser un actor importante en su región vecina significa que fue participante original del IMEC en 2023 y signataria original del Acuerdo de La Meca en 2026. Funcionarios cercanos a la casa real saudí – lo que ha sido reafirmado por Reuters – afirman que Mohammed Bin Salman, el líder titular del país, ha estado evaluando de cerca los cambios en el equilibrio de poder mundial que se alejan de los Estados Unidos y está ansioso por unirse o crear plataformas (como el BRICS+ ) que acerquen más a Arabia Saudita al sistema multilateral. El compromiso de la India con el Mediterráneo combina la expansión comercial con el cálculo estratégico. Pero, ¿la participación de la India en un conflicto entre Grecia y Turquía, así como en la ocupación israelí y el genocidio de los palestinos, beneficia al pueblo indio o simplemente sirve a los intereses de la política exterior de los Estados Unidos y la OTAN? Extender el conflicto entre la India y Pakistán al Mediterráneo introduce una nueva serie de tensiones en unas aguas que ya tienen suficientes problemas. Las ganancias de un operador portuario no constituyen una medida adecuada del interés nacional. Vijay Prashad es un historiador y periodista indio. Es autor de cuarenta libros, entre los que se incluyen Balas de Washington, Una estrella roja sobre el Tercer Mundo, Las naciones oscuras: una historia del Tercer Mundo; Las naciones pobres: una posible historia del Sur Global y How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, escrito con Grieve Chelwa. Es el director ejecutivo de Tricontinental: Instituto de Investigación Social , corresponsal jefe de Globetrotter, y editor en LeftWord Books (Nueva Delhi). También ha hecho apariciones en las películas Shadow World (2016) y Two Meetings (2017). Este artículo fue elaborado por Globetrotter .

articles.title: Will the Dems let Schumer & Jeffries sabotage the mandate?
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: A midterm blue tsunami, a total referendum on MAGA, and Democratic leaders are rushing to squander every bit of it. Rania Khalek sounds off on how Hakeem Jeffries, Chuck Schumer and “moderate” Democrats are working overtime to kill demands for Medicare for All, an end to the war on Iran, and a cutoff of weapons to Israel – before the new Congress is even sworn in Khalek explains why freshman insurgents like Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Melat Kiros won’t automatically fall in line behind Jeffries for House speaker – even as AOC keeps backing him – starting with the AIPAC money behind him. Meanwhile, incoming Rep. Don Leonard says senior House Democrats are threatening to make his life “a living hell” for attaching conditions to his vote: a vote to end Citizens United and an end to the war on Iran. And Schumer’s grip is slipping: the 600,000-member Machinists union turned against him this week, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he’s open to taking his job as Senate majority leader. But the establishment gears keep turning: as Majority Democrats meet in Denver to shape the 2028 platform, corporate media is piling on universal healthcare. Khalek breaks down why the self-styled “party of the people” is so afraid of Medicare for All — and who cashes in when it stays off the table. Khalek says the first test comes with the government funding deadline on December 11. Will Dems side with the voters who just handed them a mandate, or the donors who paid for their seats? #breakthroughnews

articles.title: A thank you note from the organisers of the 2026 Historical Materialism London Conference
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: A huge thanks to all the participants in the 2026 Historical Materialism London conference. The biggest so far with: Four full days of panels Around 1,600 participants in total 317 panels 22 parallel sessions at peak times 40 participants for the PGR conference on 4 November We would like to express our gratitude to everyone who attended the conference and brought theoretical and political work to share and debate. Together, we have sought collective ways of thinking and acting as Marxists in the broadest sense of the term in this world and conjuncture.. We would like to thank you for this huge commitment to travel (some of you from very far, at great expense, negotiating highly punitive border regimes), to take time off work, interrupt organising work, write papers whilst juggling a million other demands, in order to come here to London for these 4 very intense days. So many of you already shared with us how you gained a lot of hope, inspiration and energy from the rich and diverse presentations and the conversations you had – and how this conference serves as an anchor that reminds us that we’re not alone with the convictions from which we think and act, even if it can easily feel like that in our everyday lives and work environments. The death of our comrade, friend and co-editor Peter D. Thomas four weeks ago was a huge blow to us, but it’s a testament to our collective that we found a way to go through this and it is hugely important to carry on this work that was so central to Peter’s theoretical and political commitment. In the months that come, we will honour his legacy in many ways, up to and including organising a series of sessions on his work during next year’s conference. The success of this conference is an expression of the continuous pertinence of critical Marxist theory in these times of reaction, genocide, impending extinction, but also of resistance movements and shows that it continues to create new resources of hope. It also underlines the importance of trenchant, insightful and comradely debate among Marxists as the indispensable condition for the urgently needed new emancipatory projects. Moreover, this attendance was yet another demonstration of support and solidarity for the broader HM project, and, from our part we reiterate our commitment to improving and expanding it. There is no better proof of the growing importance of the HM project than the increasing number of HM conferences internationally. Historical Materialism SYDNEY 11-12 February 2027 https://hmsydney.org/ Radical Assembly / Historical Materialism 22-24 New York April 2027 https://radicalassembly.org/ Historical Materialism Athens 6-9 May 2027 https://hmathens.org/ The Great Transition/La Grande Transition HM Montreal 27-30 May 2027 https://thegreattransition.net/ Historical Materialism Seoul 28-30 June 2027 https://histomatesea.org/ Historical Materialism Paris 1-3 July 2027 https://hmparis.org/ Historical Materialism London 4-7 November 2027 https://www.historicalmaterialism.org/ Mexico April 2028 Brazil July 2028 At the same time, we know that the conference wasn’t perfect, so we warmly welcome comradely and constructive feedback and concrete suggestions for improvements which can be sent to conference@historicalmaterialism.org For those who require receipts and/or certificates of attendance, these will be issued in the coming week or so. Please be patient with us while we attend to this but feel free to chase us over the coming fortnight. The conference and the broader HM project cannot continue to thrive unless you help us materially, and this involves three things : Subscribing as an individual to the journal or encouraging your university libraries to take out subscriptions. For attendees of the conference, you can take advantage of a 35% discount on individual subscriptions to Historical Materialism, and gain access to 1,500 pages of cutting-edge Marxist theory each year. To subscribe, email customerservices@brill.com and mention the discount code: 71697 Buying the books in the HM Book Series, either by getting your library to buy the Brill editions ( www.brill.com/hm ) or by buying the Haymarket paperbacks ( https://www.haymarketbooks.org/series_collections/1-historical-materialism ). Particularly for those based in North America, it is worth taking a look at the Haymarket Historical Materialism book club: https://www.haymarketbooks.org/books/894-haymarket-book-club-historical-materialism-series . See also the attached discount form for Brill editions and the form for libraries. And helping us with our current crowdfunding translation projects: https://www.toledotranslationfund.org/alfred_sohn_rethel https://www.toledotranslationfund.org/christian_rakovsky_socialist_internationalist_anti_stalinist_the_definitive_biography https://www.toledotranslationfund.org/niccolomachiavelli https://www.toledotranslationfund.org/german_october_bayerlein https://www.toledotranslationfund.org/raniero_panzieri_works (We are also very happy to accept donations, bequests etc – please contact us if you want information about that.) If you gave a paper at the conference, we also encourage you to submit an article to the journal at https://www.editorialmanager.com/hima and to submit book projects to info@historicalmaterialism.org. Further details about the journal submission process can be found here: https://www.historicalmaterialism.org/instructions-for-authors . Our website https://www.historicalmaterialism.org has been upgraded and is constantly updated with new material. We welcome book reviews and other interventions for it! Do not forget to subscribe to our Newsletter which has replaced our e-mail list: https://www.historicalmaterialism.org/newsletter/ Do not forget to subscribe to our YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/@historical_materialism_journal And make sure you follow us on social media: https://www.facebook.com/groups/historicalmaterialism https://x.com/histmat?s=20 https://www.instagram.com/historical_materialism_journal/ https://bsky.app/profile/histmat.bsky.social The post A thank you note from the organisers of the 2026 Historical Materialism London Conference appeared first on Historical Materialism .
